faq.a: It is a useful screen where flow cytometry is unavailable, but a positive result should be confirmed with CD55/CD59 analysis.
faq.q: Can the acidified serum test replace flow cytometry?

faq.a: It is costly and reserved for high‑risk disease (large clone, severe hemolysis, or thrombosis) because of infection risk.
faq.q: Why is eculizumab not given to every PNH patient?

faq.a: Small clone size, recent blood transfusion, or incorrect acidification of serum can mask hemolysis.
faq.q: What causes a false‑negative acid test?

exam: A 28‑year‑old with dark urine at night and Hb 7 g/dL – which bedside test helps you decide the next step? — Perform acidified serum hemolysis test to screen for PNH before arranging flow cytometry.
Why is a positive Coombs test not sufficient to diagnose PNH? — Coombs detects antibodies, whereas PNH is complement‑mediated due to absent GPI proteins.
A patient with known PNH develops sudden abdominal pain – what is your immediate concern? — Suspect visceral vein thrombosis; order urgent CT angiography and start anticoagulation.
If flow cytometry is unavailable, how do you interpret a weakly positive acid test? — Consider a small clone; repeat test after 2 weeks and monitor LDH/hemoglobin trends.
What is the rationale for vaccinating against meningococcus before starting eculizumab? — Complement inhibition increases susceptibility to encapsulated organisms, especially Neisseria meningitidis.
Explain why washed red cells are preferred for transfusion in PNH. — Washing removes plasma complement proteins, reducing the risk of further hemolysis.
How would you differentiate G6PD deficiency from PNH in a patient with hemoglobinuria? — G6PD shows bite cells on smear and is drug‑triggered; PNH shows positive acid test and absent CD55/CD59.
A patient on eculizumab presents with fever and meningismus – what is your next action? — Treat as possible meningococcal infection; give immediate antibiotics and consider emergency vaccination.
ai.title: Acidified Serum Hemolysis Test
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: The acidified serum hemolysis test detects complement‑mediated red cell lysis, chiefly for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. It is a bedside‑compatible screen when flow cytometry is unavailable.

b: Positive test: clear supernatant after 30 min, indicating ≥5 % PNH clone.
Negative test: no hemolysis, suggesting absence of significant PNH.
sections.p: A rapid in‑vitro assay where patient serum is acidified to pH 5.5 and mixed with normal red cells; complement activation causes hemolysis if PNH clones are present.

t.b: Does the patient have complement‑mediated intravascular hemolysis? – Positive result supports PNH; negative result does not rule out small clones.
Gold‑standard confirmation of PNH clone size – use if available; otherwise rely on acid test as screening.

b: Clone <10 %: mild disease, monitor.
Clone ≥10 % with hemoglobin <8 g/dL or thrombosis: high‑risk, consider eculizumab.
sections.p: PNH severity is graded by clone size and clinical burden (hemolysis, thrombosis, marrow failure). No formal stage for the test itself.

b: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria – most common.
Acquired aplastic anemia with PNH clone – frequent in East Africa.
Rare inherited complement deficiencies – consider if family history.
sections.p: The test is positive in conditions with absent GPI‑anchored proteins on red cells, chiefly paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

b: Hemoglobinuria, especially at night.
Pallor, dyspnoea on exertion.
Abdominal or cerebral vein thrombosis.
sections.p: Patients often present with episodic dark urine, fatigue, and anemia; thrombosis in unusual sites is a red flag.

b: LDH markedly raised, haptoglobin low.
Reticulocytosis, indirect bilirubin elevation.
Renal function, urine dipstick for hemoglobin.
sections.p: Beyond the acid test, evaluate hemolysis and complications.

t.b: Is there anemia or pancytopenia? – Low Hb, possible low platelets/WBC in marrow failure.
Is hemolysis active? – LDH >2 × upper limit supports intravascular hemolysis.
Is thrombosis occurring? – Elevated D‑dimer with low fibrinogen suggests consumptive coagulopathy.

b: Acute renal failure from hemoglobin casts.
Life‑threatening venous thrombosis (hepatic, portal, cerebral).
Severe anemia causing cardiac strain.
sections.p: Uncontrolled hemolysis and thrombosis drive mortality.

b: Eculizumab or ravulizumab – complement C5 inhibitor, first‑line for high‑risk PNH.
Transfusion of washed red cells for severe anemia – avoid further complement activation.
Anticoagulation (LMWH) for documented thrombosis – balance bleeding risk.
Folic acid supplementation – supports erythropoiesis.
Avoid high‑dose vitamin C or iron overload which can exacerbate oxidative stress.
sections.p: Treat the underlying complement activation and support organ function.

b: LDH and hemoglobin every 3 months.
Flow cytometry annually if available.
Vaccinate against meningococcus before complement inhibitors.
sections.p: Regular monitoring of hemolysis markers and clone size guides therapy.

b: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia – positive Coombs test, no acid‑induced lysis.
Glucose‑6‑phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency – triggered by drugs, no complement‑mediated lysis.
Malaria – peripheral smear positive, not complement driven.
sections.p: Conditions that cause hemoglobinuria or anemia but have different mechanisms.

b: Improper pH (above 6.0) reduces complement activation.
Recent transfusion dilutes patient serum, lowering sensitivity.
sections.p: The acid test may be falsely negative in small clones or if serum is not properly acidified.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in hemoglobin >2 g/dL within 24 h
New onset severe abdominal or neurological pain suggesting thrombosis
